$comment: The rule inventory: every rule the harness enforces, and — the point of the file — where each one actually lives. `enforcedBy.kind` is the honest answer to core's own rule that a rule not in schemas/ is not a cafaye rule. `schema` means a JSON Schema constraint decides it. `doc` means a convention document states it and no schema can, so it is in this harness's source. `harness` means the rule is a fact about a filesystem or a pin rather than about a document, and lives in the named function. The set of ids here is asserted equal to RULE_IDS in harness/cafaye_contract.py, and the same set appears as a table in docs/contract-harness.md; three statements of one list, and a core test that they agree.

rules.claim: A service's cafaye.yml satisfies core's manifest schema.
A published event type starts with the publishing service's own name.
A service never consumes its own events.
Every consumed event type exists in core's catalog.
Every published event type exists in core's catalog, so a consumer is known to be waiting for it.
Every published event type has a payload schema under schemas/events/.
rules.whyCoupled: Not reachable on its own. Every type in core's catalog has a payload schema — test_every_published_fleet_event_has_a_catalog_row_and_a_payload_schema asserts exactly that — so a published type without one is necessarily a type the catalog does not list, and the two fire together. Publishing another service's type instead trips event.own-prefix and never reaches this rule. self_test.sh breakage 8 asserts both, and it is the only breakage that asserts two rules.

rules.claim: exposes.api resolves to a file inside the service repository.
The OpenAPI document declares 3.1.
info.version is present and is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and moves with the /vN prefix.
The OpenAPI document declares at least one path; an empty set is not a contract.
Every path sits under a /vN prefix.
One /vN per document; a second prefix is a breaking change that must be a decision.
A service's declared `core:` constraint admits the version core publishes.
A `core:` constraint is in the grammar the resolver accepts, and a `core:` field is present and is a string.
core's contract surface digests to the sha256 the consumer pinned, when the consumer pins one.
Core publishes exactly one readable version, so a `core:` constraint is resolvable at all.
The directory named by --core is a cafaye/core checkout, not merely a directory.
The run names where it looked for core. It never skips and exits 0.
The service root carries a cafaye.yml. An empty report's OK is not a pass.
A YAML construct outside the declared subset is refused with a file and a line, never guessed.
An SLO declaration satisfies core's SLO schema: the 28-day period, an objective that is never 100, a required description and runbook, and the two alert switches the tier alone derives.
Both SLI queries carry the literal {{.window}} token, which Sloth substitutes with each burn-rate window.
Every metric in an SLI query is one core's SLI catalogue names.
No unbounded dimension — tenant, user_id, account_id, request_id — appears in an SLI query or in one of its labels.
rules.whyCoupled: One scan, two lists, two reasons — and the reason is what a reader is owed at the moment they are about to add one. They share `_denylisted` and are deliberately NOT one rule: unbounded dimensions are barred on the 2000-combination-cap grounds metrics.schema.json already established, and infrastructure signals are barred because an SLO on them is not an SLO on behaviour. Merging them keeps the enforcement and loses the second reason. The self-test breaks both, because a rule whose reason is shared with another is a rule whose breakage could quietly depend on it.

rules.claim: No infrastructure signal — cpu, memory, pod, restart — appears in an SLI query or in one of its labels.
Each SLI query is exactly the composition of the catalogue entry it names, for this service's labels.
No SLO declaration carries a burn-rate catalog of its own; the windows are pinned once, in core.
No two SLOs in a service share a name, across files as well as within one.

notEnforced.claim: A live response validates against the event envelope and the per-type payload schema.
notEnforced.why: A contract test in PLAN.md §3's sense: it needs a running service, and core ships no runtime. darkroom's tests/contract.rs names this as what `caf contract test` was supposed to do. Still owed.

notEnforced.claim: Every service declares at least one SLO, and a `critical` or `high` one has a runbook that exists.
notEnforced.why: The harness validates the SLOs a service DECLARES: it reads `slos/*.yaml`, and a repository with no `slos/` directory is a repository that declares nothing, so it is checked on no SLO rules and passes. That is the same shape as `worker-only.cafaye.yml` declaring no `exposes.api`, and it is recorded here rather than treated as a pass over something. Nothing in the fleet declares an SLO yet — the metrics the catalogue names do not all exist — so making the directory mandatory would turn every service in the workspace red on a rule they cannot yet satisfy. It becomes enforceable the moment the first real SLO lands; until then it is written down.

notEnforced.claim: An SLI's PromQL is syntactically valid, not merely the canonical text.
notEnforced.why: PromQL parsing is `sloth validate`'s job, and Sloth is a Go binary this repository does not carry: taking it would mean core's gate reaching the network for a tool on a runner that may be air-gapped. `check_slo_sli_is_canonical` compares each query against the canonical composition as a string, which is stricter about the SHAPE and blinder about the GRAMMAR. docs/slo.md gives the pinned command for a service that has network, and DECISIONS.md D28 records the choice. Not skipped for inconvenience — the shape is checked, and the one thing left is named.

notEnforced.claim: The `core:` constraint is satisfied by a release inside the range.
notEnforced.why: core publishes no machine-readable spec version, so there is nothing on either side of the comparison. Publishing one is a core change and is listed in docs/contract-harness.md as owed.

notEnforced.claim: The OpenAPI document agrees with the service's router, and every reserved error code is used.
notEnforced.why: The document-vs-router half needs the service's language: courier reads `Router.__routes__/0` in ExUnit, muse compares against a live FastAPI app. That is a per-language test and cannot be a language-neutral harness, which is why courier's own test stays. The reserved error codes, the pagination envelope and the idempotency header are readable from a document and are still owed.

notEnforced.claim: format: uri is asserted by core's own suite.
notEnforced.why: jsonschema registers no uri checker without rfc3987-validator, so the assertion in schemas/telemetry/otel-endpoint.schema.json is vacuous in `bin/prime`. The harness checks it, which is what made the gap visible. See D22.
